ISIS claimed to have seized control of parts of Iraq's Baiji oil refinery, posting images of the assault online, though Iraqi officials denied the report and maintained that government forces remain in full control. While CNN could not independently verify the militant group's assertions, the potential damage to this critical strategic facility could significantly impact Iraq's domestic fuel supply. The refinery is located near Tikrit, a city that Iraqi forces and Shiite militias had only recently recaptured from ISIS less than two weeks prior.

Cuba has returned to the Summit of the Americas for the first time since 1962, marking a significant diplomatic shift as the United States no longer blocks its participation in the historic event. While the summit aims to advance the ongoing thaw in U.S.-Cuba relations, tensions remain high, evidenced by violent clashes between government supporters and dissidents in Panama. Key obstacles to full diplomatic normalization persist, particularly regarding Cuba's status as a state sponsor of terrorism, which Cuban officials insist must be resolved before formal ties can be fully restored.

An Alaska Airlines flight was forced to make an emergency landing shortly after takeoff when the pilot heard unusual banging from the cargo hold, which turned out to be a Menzies Aviation ramp agent who had fallen asleep inside. The plane had only been airborne for 14 minutes, and the pressurized hold ensured the employee was not in immediate danger, though he was taken to a hospital as a precaution. Alaska Airlines is currently investigating the incident after discovering that the employee’s absence was overlooked during pre-departure procedures.

One year after Boko Haram militants kidnapped nearly 300 schoolgirls in Chibok, Nigeria, most remain missing, having endured potential enslavement and abuse while their families and the global community continue to demand their return. The incident, which sparked the international #BringBackOurGirls movement, has become a symbol of the ongoing conflict, contributing to the defeat of President Goodluck Jonathan and the election of his successor, Muhammadu Buhari, who has pledged to combat the extremist group more aggressively. Following the shooting of Walter Scott by a police officer in North Charleston, artist Phillip Hyman created a hooded angel with black wings as a symbol of mourning and social justice. The artwork has been adopted by the Black Lives Matter movement, becoming a prominent icon at protests and rallies in the city. Hyman supports this usage, viewing the piece as a powerful statement on the current state of America that allows people to form their own interpretations.

Philadelphia police arrested a mother who allegedly abandoned her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in a park for four days so she could visit her boyfriend in Maryland. The son was found in critical condition with injuries including dehydration and malnutrition, leading to multiple serious charges against his mother, including aggravated assault and kidnapping. Authorities are continuing their investigation into how the young man was cared for and why family members did not intervene sooner.

After quitting a lucrative job to pursue entrepreneurship, Jia Jiang launched "100 Days of Rejection" to confront his fear of being turned down, a project that gained viral fame through his unconventional requests. This experience led to the release of his book, *Rejection Proof*, which shares his insights on transforming rejection into opportunity and overcoming the fear that often hinders success. Jiang’s story serves as a motivational example of how embracing rejection can demystify the process and open doors to unexpected possibilities.

A brood of baby ducks and their mother caused a stir in Washington, D.C., when they crossed a busy street, prompting pedestrians to stop traffic and use an umbrella to safely guide them to a grassy area. The heartwarming incident drew significant media attention, with CNN and The Washington Post covering the event as a unique occurrence in the nation's capital. Observers noted that while urban wildlife is common, such a coordinated rescue effort by strangers was an extraordinary sight.

Philadelphia police have added an attempted murder charge to the case against Nyia Parler, who left her quadriplegic son in a park for four days while she traveled to Maryland. Parler remains in custody in Maryland and cannot be extradited to face the additional charges until she completes an unspecified medical treatment. Once her treatment is finished, she will be transported to Philadelphia to face charges including aggravated assault and recklessly endangering another person.

The United States has formally complained to Moscow after a Russian fighter jet intercepted a U.S. reconnaissance plane in the Baltic Sea using what the Pentagon described as "unsafe and unprofessional" aggressive maneuvers. While Russian officials claimed the U.S. aircraft was flying toward their border with its transponder off, U.S. authorities denied this assertion and stated the incident occurred in international airspace. This event marks another instance of tense aerial encounters between the two nations, following a similarly dangerous close pass over the Sea of Okhotsk last year.

Maryland police have detained Nyia Parler, the mother of a quadriplegic man left abandoned in a Philadelphia park, and stated she cannot be extradited to face charges until she completes an unspecified medical treatment. Parler allegedly left her son, who suffers from cerebral palsy, in the woods for over four days while she traveled to Maryland to visit her boyfriend, resulting in his discovery with severe health issues including dehydration and malnutrition. Philadelphia police are awaiting the completion of her treatment before proceeding with her extradition to stand trial for the incident.

Kansas has enacted the first U.S. law banning "dismemberment abortion," a common second-trimester procedure known as dilation and evacuation, while allowing exceptions to protect the mother's life or health. The legislation has sparked intense debate, with supporters hailing it as a groundbreaking protection for life and opponents condemning it as an extreme measure that endangers women and restricts access to healthcare. As both sides prepare to challenge the law in court, advocates on both ends of the abortion rights spectrum view the statute as a potential model for future state-level policies.

Jill Duggar, the eldest daughter from the reality series "19 Kids and Counting," has become the show's first granddaughter by giving birth to a son named Israel David. The 9-pound, 10-ounce baby arrived slightly past his due date, marking a significant milestone for the Duggar family who have long documented their large household on TLC. This birth adds to the growing number of grandchildren for parents Jim Bob and Michelle Duggar, following the recent marriages and pregnancies of several other siblings.

Authorities in North Carolina are investigating whether the shooting death of a white, gay college employee at Wayne Community College was a hate crime, as the suspect is also white and may be linked to a white supremacist gang. The suspect, Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, allegedly killed his former coworker, Ron Lane, before fleeing to Florida, where he was arrested after being found sleeping on a beach. Stancil, who had been dismissed from a work-study program due to poor attendance, now faces potential charges as investigators examine the motive behind the fatal shooting.

Former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at the age of 84, prompting a wave of condolences from political and sporting figures alike. Renowned for his record-breaking career as a leg-spinner and captain, as well as his iconic commentary for the BBC, Benaud is remembered as one of Australia's most famous sporting figures. Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott announced that flags will fly at half-mast on the day of his funeral to honor his significant contribution to the nation's cultural identity.

Irish betting company Paddy Power faced significant backlash and calls for accountability after posting a tweet that compared Newcastle United's football losses to the police killings of unarmed African-American men. Although the company deleted the tweet and claimed it was intended as a harmless joke, social media users condemned the comparison, arguing that the offensive content warranted serious consequences. This incident adds to a history of controversial publicity stunts by the firm, drawing sharp criticism for its insensitivity regarding recent racial tensions in the United States.

The Italian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean Sea on Friday, contributing to a sharp increase in arrivals from Africa and the Middle East as of 2015. According to the International Organization for Migration, at least 480 people have died during these crossings this year, a significant rise from the previous year, largely due to overcrowded vessels and dangerous conditions. Most of those arriving are asylum seekers, trafficking victims, or vulnerable individuals using Libya as a transit point to reach Europe.

President Barack Obama reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring Israel maintains a qualitative military edge over Iran, aiming to address Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s concerns regarding the recent nuclear deal. While acknowledging the Israeli leader's skepticism about trusting Tehran, Obama argued that the agreement offers a unique opportunity to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons through strict limits and increased inspections. Despite criticism from Netanyahu and Republican lawmakers, the administration maintains that the deal provides necessary clarity and security for the region while negotiations for a final draft continue until June 30.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage, including genres like morna and funana, as a key driver for economic development in the absence of traditional natural resources. The government and cultural leaders view the creative economy as a vital alternative sector, supported by successful initiatives like the Kriol Jazz Festival that attract international talent and tourism. Despite being a relatively small part of the current economy, these cultural assets show promising potential for long-term growth and global recognition.

New research published in *Psychological Science* suggests that "Double Falsehood," a play long attributed to 18th-century writer Lewis Theobald, was actually written by William Shakespeare with assistance from John Fletcher. By using computer software to analyze the "psychological signatures" of the authors, researchers found that the language patterns in the play match Shakespeare’s style so closely that it is likely his work. This scientific approach may finally settle the historical debate regarding the play's authorship, which many scholars had previously dismissed as a forgery.

Following a deadly Al-Shabaab attack on a Kenyan university that killed 147 people, the Kenyan government has frozen dozens of bank accounts linked to suspected terror supporters. While authorities face criticism for their response to the siege, they have also launched airstrikes against militant training camps in Somalia and offered a reward for information leading to the attack's organizer. The tragedy has sparked national mourning and social media campaigns highlighting the lives of the victims, who were predominantly students.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of early release for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend, Travis Alexander, after a judge determined that the severity of the crime warranted serving her entire sentence. Although Arias expressed deep remorse during the sentencing hearing, the court proceeded with life imprisonment because two separate juries failed to reach a unanimous decision regarding the death penalty. The convicted killer will serve her time at the Arizona State Prison Complex-Perryville, marking the conclusion of a high-profile legal case that spanned several years.

Chinese authorities have formally detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for planning International Women's Day protests against sexual harassment, with their legal status set to be determined by April 13. The detentions occur ironically during a year marking the 20th anniversary of Beijing's influential Fourth World Conference on Women and just before the potential adoption of China's first anti-domestic violence law. These activists are recognized for using creative direct action to challenge both government rights violations and entrenched gender norms within Chinese society.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid, discovered in 2010, after Malala Yousafzai to honor the teenage activist's advocacy for girls' education. Mainzer chose to name the celestial body 316201 Malala because very few asteroids have been designated to recognize the contributions of women, particularly women of color. The scientist emphasized that recognizing Malala’s work is logical, as educating half the global population is essential for solving humanity's most difficult problems.

Emy Afalava, a decorated veteran born in American Samoa, is suing the federal government to secure U.S. citizenship and voting rights, arguing that the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees these rights to those born on U.S. soil. The article highlights the historical context of this legal battle, noting that racial discrimination has previously led to the denial of full constitutional protections for residents of U.S. territories, such as in the *Dred Scott* and *Gonzalez* cases. The recent Ebola epidemic, described as the most severe public health emergency in modern times, has resulted in over 10,000 deaths and exposed significant vulnerabilities in global government systems. Although the intensity of the outbreak has decreased with weekly cases hitting their lowest point since May 2014, the virus remains active, with mixed progress seen across affected countries. While some nations like Liberia have reduced case numbers to the point of decommissioning treatment facilities, others like Guinea continue to struggle with hidden transmission chains and unsafe burial practices.

Attorney General Eric Holder has issued a memo to all U.S. Justice Department personnel reiterating that soliciting prostitution is strictly prohibited, regardless of local laws or whether agents are on duty. This directive follows recent inspector general reports highlighting misconduct by federal agents, including DEA and Secret Service members, who were involved in scandals involving paid sex with prostitutes in foreign countries. Holder emphasized that violating this rule will result in suspension or termination, aiming to protect the department's core mission and combat human trafficking.

Nashville’s district attorney has banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals after such offers were made four times in the past five years, sparking public outrage and comparisons to historical eugenics practices. The article argues that while these modern plea deals evoke the dark history of forced sterilization, they differ legally because they involve voluntary choices by defendants rather than involuntary state mandates. Ultimately, the author suggests that even if sterilization were deemed an unconstitutional punishment, it might still be permissible within a plea agreement if the defendant willingly consents to it.

Following Dzhokhar Tsarnaev’s conviction for the Boston Marathon bombing, the article argues that preventing future violence requires understanding the specific drivers of radicalization rather than blaming Islam itself. It posits that radicalization stems from a complex intersection of politics, religious identity, and perceived global injustices against Muslim communities, such as conflicts in Afghanistan, Chechnya, and Palestine. Ultimately, the text suggests that addressing these underlying political grievances is essential to stopping young men from being drawn into extremism.

The shooting of Walter Scott by police officer Michael Slager in South Carolina sparked national outrage and Slager's arrest after a bystander's video contradicted the officer's initial false account of the incident. However, the case highlights a critical failure in federal law enforcement, as a 1994 statute requiring the collection of data on police killings has never been properly implemented. This lack of comprehensive data prevents a clear understanding of how often such incidents occur and whether they correlate with specific training, bias, or stress factors.

Apple has released a new mobile operating system update featuring a significantly more diverse range of emojis, including various skin tones, same-sex couples, and an expanded selection of national flags. While the update has been widely praised for promoting inclusivity and representation, it has also sparked controversy and criticism from conservative figures and specific minority groups who feel excluded, such as redheads and Armenians. The announcement highlights the cultural significance of digital representation, illustrating how even small changes in technology can ignite broader societal debates about identity and acceptance.

Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential candidacy places an unprecedented burden on her to serve as the primary barometer for gender equality in the United States, regardless of the election's outcome. A victory risks creating a false sense of accomplishment that halts broader progress for women in politics, while a defeat could reinforce damaging myths about female electability and discourage future women candidates. Ultimately, the article argues that Clinton’s unique, high-profile status makes it flawed to use her specific campaign results as a general referendum on the viability of women in leadership.

This week features six notable television premieres, headlined by the debut of "A.D. The Bible Continues" on NBC, which serves as a sequel to the 2013 hit "The Bible." Other highlights include the final episodes of "Mad Men" on AMC, the return of "Louie" and "The Comedians" on FX, and the launch of Marvel's "Daredevil" on Netflix. Additionally, NBC airs the new drama "American Odyssey," rounding out a diverse lineup of new and returning series.

The Pentagon released a map indicating that coalition forces have reclaimed 25-30% of Iraqi territory from ISIS, though experts caution that these gains are part of a dynamic conflict where territory frequently changes hands. Counterinsurgency specialist Afzal Ashraf argues that while the territorial losses damage ISIS's prestige, the group continues to adapt through asymmetric warfare and spectacular attacks to maintain its image of initiative. Furthermore, Ashraf criticizes the current coalition strategy as a conventional frontal push rather than a more effective maneuverist approach that could disrupt ISIS's command and control structures.

Arsenal kept their slim Premier League title hopes alive by defeating Burnley 1-0, moving within four points of leaders Chelsea ahead of a crucial upcoming clash. The victory highlights Arsenal's impressive eight-game winning streak, driven by the defensive midfield contributions of Francis Coquelin. Meanwhile, results at the bottom of the table saw Aston Villa secure a vital win over Tottenham, while Sunderland suffered a heavy defeat to Crystal Palace.

The author argues that the tragic shooting of Walter Scott by Officer Michael Slager highlights the critical need for police body cameras, suggesting that such technology could have prevented the incident by ensuring accountability and transparency. While acknowledging the financial costs of implementing these devices, the article contends that the expense is justified by the potential to save lives, reduce civil liabilities, and restore public trust in law enforcement. Ultimately, the piece posits that body cameras serve as a vital interim solution to break the cycle of fear and tension between police and minority communities, even as they expose deeper systemic biases within the criminal justice system.

While recent statistics show that most Americans receive substantial tax refunds and benefit from simplified, free filing processes, the underlying U.S. tax system remains deeply flawed. The article argues that these short-term financial benefits mask serious structural issues, including biases against two-worker marriages and a system that disproportionately favors the wealthy through limited taxes on capital. Ultimately, the author suggests that the public's focus on immediate refunds distracts from these significant inequities in the tax code.

The Yarmouk refugee camp in Damascus has become a focal point of Syria's civil war, suffering catastrophic destruction and severe humanitarian crises due to intense fighting between government forces, rebel groups, and ISIS. Since the recent ISIS incursion, the area has been besieged, leaving approximately 18,000 remaining residents without adequate food, water, or access to international aid. The conflict has resulted in massive civilian casualties and widespread displacement, highlighting the senseless loss of life and the scale of destruction in this once-thriving community.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards delivered a mix of memorable highlights and notable misfires, headlined by Amy Schumer’s inventive opening monologue and Channing Tatum’s surprise twerk for Jennifer Lopez. While performances by Fall Out Boy and Charli XCX were praised for their energy, the event also featured awkward moments such as Schumer’s archery fail and a controversial "Gone Girl" joke. Ultimately, the ceremony was defined by its blend of high-energy comedy and occasional stumbles, with standout performances from Kevin Hart and Robert Downey Jr. rounding out the night.

Marvel Studios and other major franchises recently revealed new character details and visuals for upcoming superhero films, including the full look of the Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron," the real Daredevil suit, and casting news for "X-Men: Apocalypse" and "Fantastic Four." These announcements, which also included images of Angel and The Thing, highlight the continued momentum and popularity of the superhero genre. The rapid succession of these reveals underscores that the trend of blockbuster superhero movies shows no signs of slowing down.

Former New England Patriots player Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison for the 2013 shooting death of Odin Lloyd. During the sentencing hearing, Lloyd’s grieving family members delivered emotional victim impact statements, describing him as a dedicated athlete and the backbone of their family. The proceedings marked the conclusion of a more than two-year legal battle for Lloyd's relatives, who expressed profound loss while honoring his memory and character.

Former New England Patriots star Aaron Hernandez faces multiple upcoming legal proceedings, including a postponed double-murder trial and two civil lawsuits, despite his recent conviction in the death of Odin Lloyd. Prosecutors allege Hernandez killed two men and wounded others in a 2012 shooting, while civil suits involve claims from a man shot in Miami and the families of the victims seeking damages. Additionally, Hernandez’s legal team must navigate a dispute over unpaid NFL bonus money, meaning he will require representation from various attorneys across these distinct criminal and civil matters.

Tatiana Maslany stars in the highly anticipated return of "Orphan Black," which introduces male clones and promises more complex cloning scenes as it premieres on BBC America. The week's television lineup also features significant developments for other popular series, including the second season of "Turn: Washington's Spies" and the fifth season of "Game of Thrones." Additionally, viewers can look forward to the season finales of "Justified" and "Nurse Jackie," as well as new episodes of "Veep."

Actress Alyssa Milano expressed anger on social media after Heathrow Airport authorities allegedly confiscated her pumped breast milk and the cooler it was stored in. Although UK Department of Transport regulations allow travelers to carry breast milk in quantities larger than 100ml, airport staff reportedly enforced a guideline limiting passengers to only what is needed for the flight. This incident mirrors a similar controversy from 2011 involving another mother at the same airport.

Ten years after Centre County, Pennsylvania, prosecutor Ray Gricar vanished, his case remains one of the most perplexing missing persons stories in the United States, with investigators having exhausted numerous leads without finding him. While police have discovered his abandoned car and damaged laptop, the prevailing theories suggest he either committed suicide or deliberately disappeared, a notion supported by online searches regarding hard drive destruction. Despite extensive efforts involving over 300 sightings and DNA comparisons, no definitive evidence has emerged to confirm whether Gricar fell victim to foul play or intentionally erased his past.

Marking the 150th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's death, this article argues that his commitment to preserving the Union and ending slavery was deeply rooted in his Midwestern identity and geographic understanding. It highlights Lincoln's belief that the United States was a single, indivisible nation created by the federal government, contrasting his national perspective with the state-centric views of Southerners like Robert E. Lee. Ultimately, the piece asserts that Lincoln's legacy is inseparable from his origins in the Midwest, where he witnessed firsthand the economic and political necessity of a unified country.

Marvel's "Daredevil" has premiered on Netflix to strong critical acclaim, with 94% positive reviews on Rotten Tomatoes praising its faithful adaptation and well-choreographed action. Critics and early viewers have particularly highlighted Charlie Cox’s performance as the blind attorney Matt Murdock and the show's decision to skip a lengthy origin story. While the series is already considered a hit, it remains to be seen if it can sustain the long-term success of Netflix's previous hits like "House of Cards."

Ringling Bros. has announced it will phase out elephants from its traveling circus and expand its conservation center in Polk City, Florida, following years of legal challenges and inconsistent local regulations. The decision allows the circus to focus on its 200-acre sanctuary, which now serves as a breeding ground and research facility for a sustainable herd of Asian elephants. This move aims to ensure the species' survival through advanced conservation efforts, including cryo-preservation, while avoiding the financial burden of ongoing litigation.

Two years after the Boston Marathon bombings, the city held somber "One Boston Day" ceremonies to honor the victims and survivors, marking a moment of resilience and remembrance for the community. Meanwhile, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who was recently convicted on 30 charges related to the attacks, awaits sentencing next week with the death penalty under consideration. The events served as a tribute to the city's strength, bringing together families of those lost, survivors, and residents to reflect on the tragedy and the spirit of Boston.

Panic at the University of Nairobi’s Kikuyu campus resulted in one death and hundreds of injuries after students mistook explosions from a faulty electrical cable for a terror attack. The incident triggered a stampede in which some students jumped from a fifth-floor dormitory, causing significant harm amidst heightened fears following a recent Al-Shabaab massacre. University officials have confirmed the cause was an electrical issue and are working to restore power while urging the community to remain calm.

Tulsa County reserve deputy Robert Bates turned himself in and posted bail after being charged with second-degree manslaughter for fatally shooting Eric Courtney Harris during an undercover sting operation. While authorities claim Bates inadvertently fired his gun instead of deploying his Taser, Harris’s family and attorneys argue that excessive force was unnecessary given that multiple officers had already subdued the suspect. The incident has sparked public criticism regarding the involvement of a volunteer reserve deputy with limited training in a high-risk situation, leading to calls for an independent investigation.

Sisters Iman and Siham Hashi, known collectively as Faarrow, are launching their musical careers in Los Angeles with a debut album that blends Afro-pop, hip hop, and African percussion. The refugee sisters, who fled Somalia as children and relocated to Canada, are working with producer Elijah Kelley to bring their unique sound to the world while maintaining a strong connection to their humanitarian efforts. Their journey from Mogadishu to the global music stage highlights their passion for blending diverse musical influences with their personal history and advocacy for refugees.

Hundreds of additional Iraqi troops and paramilitary forces have been deployed to reinforce defenses at the Baiji oil refinery against an ongoing ISIS assault. Although ISIS claimed to have taken control of parts of the facility, Iraqi officials maintain that their forces are holding their ground and preparing to repel the attackers. This strategic reinforcement aims to protect a critical source of fuel for Iraq, as the conflict threatens to disrupt domestic energy supplies.

Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) has abandoned efforts to retrieve a robotic probe that became stuck inside one of the damaged reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant. Although the robot successfully collected radiation data at 14 of 18 target locations before being blocked by debris, TEPCO decided to cut its tethering cable after it had covered two-thirds of its planned route. This incident highlights the ongoing challenges and high costs associated with decommissioning the facility, which remains too hazardous for human entry four years after the 2011 disaster.

A Saudi official reported that more than 500 Houthi rebels have been killed and 1,200 airstrikes conducted since the start of the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. The conflict has resulted in significant casualties on both sides, with three Saudi soldiers killed in recent border clashes and hundreds of Yemeni civilians reported dead or wounded. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization estimates a much higher toll, including militant casualties, as Yemen continues to face a severe humanitarian crisis.

A Hong Kong bakery, Jenny's, has sparked a massive craze for its butter cookies, leading to long lines, a booming black market, and the proliferation of counterfeit products. The high demand has resulted in scalpers reselling the treats at significant markups, prompting the original store to issue warnings against buying these "fake" versions. This phenomenon is part of a broader global trend of fleeting food manias, such as cronuts and ramen burgers, that capture public attention before quickly fading.

A suicide bombing by a woman outside a bus station in Gombe, Nigeria, killed at least five people and injured more than a dozen others. Although no group has claimed responsibility, Boko Haram remains the primary suspect, as the group has increasingly targeted soft civilian sites following recent military setbacks. This attack marks the first major incident since Nigeria's recent presidential election, which saw opposition candidate Muhammadu Buhari win with a pledge to defeat the insurgents.

Brett McGurk, the Obama administration’s counter-ISIS coordinator, described the threat as historically unprecedented, noting that the number of foreign fighters in Syria is twice that of the Soviet-Afghan war. As the U.S.-led coalition expands its operations to include countries like Canada and targets ISIS affiliates in Libya and Yemen, the administration is also focusing on engaging Sunni tribes in Iraq to bolster local offensives. Despite ISIS's global appeal, McGurk emphasized that the group's violent reality in Syria and Iraq is increasingly deterring foreign fighters through high casualty rates.

The first trailer for the documentary "Amy: The Girl Behind the Name" has been released, offering a glimpse into the life and music of the late British singer Amy Winehouse. Endorsed by her family and directed by Asif Kapadia, the film aims to present a sensitive and honest tribute to her legacy, distinguishing itself from previous projects by featuring extensive unseen archive footage. While the documentary is set for a UK release on July 3, a U.S. release date has yet to be announced.

Federal Judge George A. O’Toole has ordered the jury in Dzhokhar Tsarnaev’s trial to avoid attending the upcoming Boston Marathon or any related anniversary events to prevent prejudice during the sentencing phase. The jury recently convicted Tsarnaev on all 30 counts, including the use of weapons of mass destruction, following a trial where his defense argued he acted under his brother's influence. The sentencing phase is scheduled to begin on April 21, immediately after this year's marathon, with the judge cautioning that the process could last up to four weeks.

Former U.S. Army enlistee John T. Booker Jr. was arrested and charged with attempting to detonate a car bomb at Fort Riley in Kansas after posting extremist messages on Facebook. The plot was thwarted by confidential informants who provided a device made of nonexplosive materials, ensuring that no one was in danger and base security was never breached. Booker, who had recently been discharged from the Army, confessed to agents that he intended to carry out an insider attack inspired by the Fort Hood shooting.

Actress Gwyneth Paltrow participated in the #FoodBankNYCChallenge by purchasing a week's worth of groceries for just under $30, demonstrating the limited purchasing power of food stamp benefits. Nominated by celebrity chef Mario Batali, the initiative urges participants to live on a $29 weekly budget to raise awareness about the financial struggles faced by families relying on government assistance. The challenge aims to highlight the impact of recent food stamp cuts and encourage empathy for those who cannot afford adequate nutrition.

During a practice session at Creve Coeur Lake, the Washington University rowing team was suddenly attacked by a swarm of Asian carp that leaped into their boat. Team member Devin Patel recounted the terrifying experience of struggling with a slippery, flopping fish on his legs, though fortunately, no injuries occurred. The incident left the rowers unharmed but reminded them of the lingering strong smell of fish after the chaotic event.

In a historic victory that marks the first time an opposition party has defeated the ruling party in Nigeria's democratic elections, Muhammadu Buhari has been elected president, defeating incumbent Goodluck Jonathan. Buhari has pledged to aggressively combat corruption and coordinate with neighboring nations to curb violence from the terrorist group Boko Haram in the northeast. Following a peaceful transition of power, Buhari is set to be sworn in on May 29, aiming to address the country's critical security and economic challenges.

ISIS fighters have seized control of eastern Ramadi, Iraq, cutting off the last safe route for civilians to flee to Baghdad and forcing thousands to escape on foot across the Euphrates River. The sudden collapse of local security has resulted in a chaotic exodus of exhausted and traumatized residents, while government officials warn that the city's defenses are failing. As ISIS advances, wounded fighters and desperate civilians recount stories of being displaced from their homes with no military backup arriving to defend them.

Amina Ali Qassim and her family narrowly escaped the destruction of their home in Yemen by fleeing across the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti in a crowded boat, an ordeal they described as a "window into hell." While the U.N. prepares for thousands more refugees arriving in Djibouti, Qassim remains deeply worried about her daughters, who are still trapped in the conflict zone in Taiz. The family now faces life in temporary plastic shelters, possessing only the few items they could carry away from their destroyed lives.

Georgia Governor Nathan Deal has signed "Haleigh's Hope Act," a bill that legalizes low-THC cannabis oil for treating specific forms of medication-resistant epilepsy. The legislation was championed by the family of five-year-old Haleigh Cox, whose life was saved by medical marijuana after she moved to Colorado, prompting her family to return home now that the treatment is available in Georgia. This law allows patients with covered conditions to access in-state care, ending the need for families to travel to other states for life-saving treatment.

Photographer Carolina Sandretto documents life in Cuba’s "solares," crumbling communal housing where multiple families cohabitate due to post-revolution housing shortages, offering a stark contrast to the island's typical tourist imagery. Through persistent engagement and the use of vintage equipment, she captures intimate, unvarnished scenes of daily existence within these unique social habitats. Sandretto hopes to continue chronicling these evolving living conditions as diplomatic changes and increased tourism potentially reshape life in the solares.

The White House maintains that it does not require congressional approval for the Iran nuclear deal, opting instead to proceed as a nonbinding executive agreement to avoid political hurdles. However, critics argue that securing legislative consent would create a more enduring and legitimate diplomatic breakthrough, despite the significant political effort required. Meanwhile, bipartisan legislation is advancing on Capitol Hill to mandate a congressional review process, challenging the administration's current approach.

Lady Antebellum singer Hillary Scott and her crew were safely evacuated from a tour bus that caught fire on a Texas freeway after a rear tire blew out. While the incident destroyed the back lounge of the vehicle, including most of their belongings, the band members confirmed that everyone on board was unharmed. The group remains scheduled to perform at the upcoming Academy of Country Music Awards in Arlington, Texas.

The Senate passed a bipartisan Medicare reform bill with a 92-8 vote, permanently resolving the "doc fix" to prevent immediate payment cuts to physicians and extending a children's health insurance program. While the legislation received strong support from both parties and was expected to be signed by President Obama, it faced criticism from some conservative senators who argued the bill was too costly and expanded existing healthcare policies. The House had already approved the same measure, ensuring that the urgent issue of provider payments was addressed before the scheduled deadline.

After finding an engraved ring in a Bali rip current, Australian woman Roxy Walsh used social media to track down its owners, Joe and Jenny Langley. The Langleys' granddaughter recognized the post, leading to a successful reunion where Walsh returned the sentimental item to the couple in Noosa. This heartwarming story highlights how digital sharing can bridge vast distances to restore cherished personal connections.

The militant group, Ansar Beit Al-Maqdis, claimed responsibility for a car bomb explosion in Al-Arish and an ambush on a highway, marking a significant escalation in the decade-long insurgency. She was a stabilizing force for John during the early years of the Beatles' rise to fame, though their marriage ended in divorce in 1968 as the band's overwhelming fame created significant challenges for their family life. Stiviano to repay former Clippers owner Donald Sterling more than $2.6 million in gifts, including luxury cars and real estate, following a lawsuit filed by Sterling’s wife. Shelly Sterling argued that her husband’s wealth was misused to benefit Stiviano, a claim the court accepted as a victory for the family in recovering these assets. This legal ruling follows the NBA’s previous decision to strip Donald Sterling of his team ownership due to racist remarks he made against Stiviano regarding her social media interactions with African-Americans.

Iranian-American journalist Jason Rezaian, the Washington Post’s bureau chief in Tehran, faces imminent trial on charges of economic spying that US officials and his employer have firmly dismissed as absurd. Rezaian has been detained since July without proper legal representation or bail, while his wife was released on bail in October. Despite appeals from figures like Muhammad Ali and ongoing protests from the State Department and the Post, Rezaian remains imprisoned as his family and supporters continue to demand his immediate release.

NBA player Thabo Sefolosha has announced that he will miss the rest of the season, including the playoffs, after suffering a significant leg injury during his arrest by New York police. Sefolosha claims the injury, which includes a fractured fibula and ligament damage, was caused by the officers, though police maintain he was not involved in a separate stabbing incident nearby. His opponent, Tigran Petrosian, grew suspicious of Nigalidze’s frequent bathroom breaks during crucial moments of the game, leading to an investigation that uncovered the device and logged-in accounts. Al Qaeda has suffered a significant deterioration in its leadership following the recent deaths of key figures Ustad Ahmad Farooq and Qari Abdullah Mansur in CIA drone strikes, leaving only top leader Ayman al-Zawahiri. These losses highlight the group's transformation into a largely Pakistan-focused organization with virtually no capacity to execute major attacks in the West. While its affiliate, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, remains a threat, the core al Qaeda organization is now significantly weakened compared to its rival, ISIS.

A report alleges that supervisors at the Tulsa County Sheriff's Office were ordered to forge training records for Reserve Deputy Robert Bates, who killed a suspect during a sting operation, with three officials allegedly reassigned for refusing. While the Sheriff’s Office denies these claims and questions the credibility of the anonymous sources, the incident has intensified scrutiny over Bates' qualifications and the department's handling of volunteer police programs. Bates maintains he accidentally discharged his firearm instead of using his Taser, but the controversy highlights significant gaps in his documented training and certification records.

TV5Monde, a French-language global television network, experienced a significant cyberattack that caused eleven of its channels to go offline along with its websites and social media accounts. While the network stated it was hacked by an "Islamist group" and ISIS logos appeared on some platforms, no group has officially claimed responsibility for the attack. Hillary Clinton’s campaign-in-waiting has distributed a "values statement" outlining its core principles and strategy, aiming to avoid the mistakes that plagued her 2008 presidential run. The document emphasizes humility, discipline, and unity, explicitly stating that the campaign is focused on the collective effort rather than just Clinton herself. By obtaining a driver's license and Social Security card, Helinski was able to access his long-accumulated Social Security benefits and a dormant bank account. The blast, which occurred while a front loader was operating near the site, caused a massive fire and resulted in serious injuries such as burns and conditions requiring emergency surgery for some victims. Thousands of South Africans rallied in Durban against recent xenophobic violence that has resulted in five deaths, with many using social media hashtags to voice their support for peace. However, some activists argue that online advocacy is insufficient, prompting individuals like Tim Flack to file formal complaints with the Human Rights Commission regarding hate speech by political figures. Prosecutors allege that Moschetto, along with two accomplices, attempted to commit arson against the rival's office and provided funds and prescriptions to facilitate the attack. All three defendants have pleaded not guilty and were released on bail following their arraignment in Nassau County.

The U.N. Security Council has approved an arms embargo and sanctions targeting the Houthis and supporters of former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh to curb their military advance and influence. While Saudi Arabia leads a coalition conducting airstrikes against these groups, Egypt has agreed to send naval ships to assist, though officials clarified that no ground troops have been deployed yet. The resolution aims to raise the cost for the rebels and address concerns regarding Iranian influence in Yemen, despite Russia abstaining from the vote due to objections to the sanctions.

A trailer for Zack Snyder's "Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice" was briefly leaked online before being quickly removed, revealing scenes of the two titular heroes coming face to face. The unauthorized upload, which featured Spanish subtitles, appeared just days before the official premiere scheduled for Monday in IMAX theaters. The highly anticipated film, starring Ben Affleck and Henry Cavill, is set for release on March 25, 2016.

Former NFL star Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole after a months-long trial involving extensive evidence and witness testimony. Following the verdict, jurors described the deliberation process as the hardest thing they had ever done, emphasizing that they reached their conclusion based solely on the evidence presented in court. The case marks a significant legal milestone for Hernandez, who now faces additional criminal and civil proceedings related to other alleged crimes.

The incident, which occurred in broad daylight and was captured on video, has led to the suspension of the two previously arrested students from their respective universities and track team. Authorities continue to investigate the case, emphasizing that such behavior is unacceptable, while planning to interview the victim to potentially identify other individuals involved in the assault.

The Defense Department announced that remains of up to nearly 400 unaccounted-for service members from the USS Oklahoma will be exhumed this year in an effort to identify and return them to their families. This initiative aims to provide closure to the relatives of the 429 sailors and Marines who died when the battleship sank during the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor. Next of kin have begun receiving notifications, with identified service members set to be returned for burial with full military honors.

Although her family was debriefed and she was subsequently released into their care, officials emphasized that preventing the recruitment of young people into terrorist groups remains a critical priority.

This indirect approach allowed the Vatican to acknowledge the tragedy while maintaining diplomatic continuity with Turkey, which disputes the characterization of the deaths as genocide. Peterson, who was suspended in November for disciplining his four-year-old son with a switch, must now adhere to strict conditions including ongoing counseling and adherence to the league's personal conduct policy. The Vikings have expressed their eagerness for Peterson to rejoin the team, though it remains unclear if he will attend upcoming voluntary workouts.

Police state that Bates, who was part of a violent crimes task force, intended to use a Taser but mistakenly discharged his service weapon while Harris was resisting arrest. The suspect later died at a hospital, and an investigation is underway to determine the exact circumstances of the shooting.

Authorities continue to face challenges from online drug trafficking and have intensified efforts to regulate drug use within the entertainment industry through stricter bans and legal consequences.

Polish photographer Tomasz Lazar has documented the harrowing stories of elderly Poles who were deported to Siberia as children by Soviet authorities during World War II. Through intimate interviews and portraits, Lazar captures the enduring trauma of these survivors, many of whom only recently felt safe enough to share their experiences after the fall of the Soviet Union. The project serves as a historical record intended to preserve these personal narratives and remind future generations of the atrocities committed against them.

The article argues that this widespread culture of silence forces women to restrict their daily activities, urging a societal shift where women acknowledge their collective power to confront and change these behaviors.

Canadian actor Jonathan Crombie, best known for his role as Gilbert Blythe in the beloved "Anne of Green Gables" television series, died this week at the age of 48 due to complications from a brain hemorrhage. Producer Kevin Sullivan remembered Crombie as a dedicated actor who brought significant depth to the character, noting the strong on-screen chemistry he shared with co-star Megan Follows. Although Crombie appeared in various other productions, he remained deeply proud of his iconic portrayal of Gilbert, which continues to resonate with fans worldwide.

This shift is attributed to the group's significant weakening in Somalia due to sustained pressure from African Union forces, as well as covert U.S. drone strikes and special operations that have decimated its leadership and territorial control. Consequently, the attack serves as a desperate attempt by an unraveling organization to maintain relevance despite its declining capabilities.

During the hearing, Judge Ronald Coen lowered Knight's bail to $10 million and dismissed one of the hit-and-run counts, citing legal restrictions on multiple charges involving the same vehicle. Knight, who faces up to life in prison, appeared in court despite recent health struggles, while the sole surviving victim, Cle Sloan, has refused to testify against him.

During National Park Week, which runs from April 18 through April 26, 128 U.S. national parks that typically charge an entrance fee will offer free admission on Saturday and Sunday. The National Park Service and National Park Foundation are hosting various events, including astronomy parties and Junior Ranger activities, to encourage public exploration. Visitors are invited to discover nearby parks via FindYourPark.com and share their experiences using the hashtag #FindYourPark.

This local struggle reflects a broader national issue, with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development estimating that 7.7 million low-income households spend more than half their income on rent or live in substandard housing. In response, HUD is implementing initiatives to preserve existing affordable housing and fund repairs through private investment, while urging Congress to expand these programs to prevent further loss of critical housing units.

Debra Lobo, a 55-year-old American vice principal at a medical school in Karachi, Pakistan, was shot in the head and arm by two assailants on a motorcycle while driving home. Although she is currently unconscious, police report that she is expected to survive the attack, which was accompanied by pamphlets calling for America to be burned. The U.S. Consulate General in Karachi is cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.

A jury of Rolling Stone’s media peers has condemned the magazine’s discredited story about a University of Virginia rape as "journalistic malpractice," citing severe lapses in reporting and editing. The investigation revealed that the publication failed to verify key facts, ignored red flags from their source, and refused to give the accused fraternity a chance to respond before publishing. While the errors are described as regrettable, the jury criticized the magazine’s decision to take no disciplinary action or reorganize its newsroom in response to the scandal.

Jon Cryer reprised his iconic record-store dance from the 1986 film *Pretty in Pink* during a recent episode of "The Late Late Show with James Corden." The actor performed the routine alongside host James Corden, who expressed his excitement about fulfilling a childhood dream by recreating the scene. The segment highlighted the enduring appeal of the classic John Hughes film among its now middle-aged fanbase.

Through this project, Dumig aims to universalize Sah’s story, emphasizing the shared human emotions and dignity that connect people despite their physical separation and bureaucratic struggles. The situation escalated when a police officer deliberately rammed Valencia’s vehicle with his patrol car to stop the crime spree, an action that has sparked nationwide debate regarding the officer's justification. Valencia was hospitalized and subsequently jailed, where he now faces 15 charges including shoplifting and armed robbery.

The EPA has confirmed the presence of methyl bromide, a restricted and highly toxic chemical, in the unit where the family was staying, leading to an ongoing investigation into potential regulatory violations. While the boys are in critical condition and their father cannot move, their mother has been released from the hospital and is undergoing occupational therapy.

All U.S. Consulate personnel were reported safe and accounted for after the vehicle detonated before reaching the building. The U.S. State Department praised the response of the Kurdish government and pledged continued cooperation in combating terrorist acts in the region.

While the government has condemned the violence and praised police efforts to restore order, the unrest stems from local residents' anger over perceived job competition with immigrants from other African nations. This incident echoes previous anti-immigrant tensions in South Africa, prompting both government officials and charities to urge citizens to remember the country's own history of seeking refuge on the continent.

As the death toll mounts, fears are growing that the violence is escalating into a broader proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran for regional dominance. Meanwhile, the UN Security Council has imposed an arms embargo and sanctions on the Houthis in an attempt to curb the violence and restore stability.

The theatre maintains that her salary is consistent with her role and local exchange rates, while Womack asserts she is treated equally to her Russian counterparts.

Despite the arrest of some co-conspirators and the intervention of a friend who became an FBI informant, the remaining suspects continued their plot for ten months, attempting to find creative ways to leave the country. They have been held without bail as they face federal charges for their involvement in the terrorist conspiracy.

Dr. Sanjay Gupta has released a three-part CNN documentary series, "Weed 3: The Marijuana Revolution," to address public questions and misconceptions surrounding medical marijuana. The series explores the potential benefits for conditions such as PTSD, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain, while also acknowledging legitimate concerns regarding long-term effects on the developing brain. Gupta aims to bridge the gap between scientific research and public understanding by highlighting ongoing studies and challenging the historical taboo that has kept the topic out of medical education.

In July, Sierra Sharry and Lane Smith were expecting a baby. Sharry was eight months pregnant when Smith fell and hit his head. He was taken to a hospital in Oklahoma City, but he never recovered. Sharry said on Facebook that July 13, 2014, was the worst day of her life because she lost her best friend and the father of her unborn child. Their son, Taos, was born a few weeks later. When it was time for Taos’s six-month photos, Sharry asked the photographer to help make the family look complete in just one picture.

People have strong opinions about Indiana’s new religious freedom law. Some people are angry, saying the law allows businesses to treat gay and lesbian customers unfairly by hiding behind religion. Others, like Indiana Governor Mike Pence, are surprised by the anger. They argue that the law is not new; it is very similar to laws already existing in Washington, D.C., and 19 other states. The debate is intense because people disagree on what the law really means and what its true purpose is.

Some fans of Lucille Ball want a statue of her removed from a park in her hometown, Celoron, New York. They say the statue looks ugly and does not look like the "I Love Lucy" star. Since it was put up in 2009, the life-size bronze statue has been compared to singer Conway Twitty, the snake from the movie "Beetlejuice," and actor Steve Buscemi. Even the mayor, Scott Schrecengost, does not like the statue, which shows Lucille Ball holding a bottle of a fictional drink called Vitameatavegamin. Despite these complaints, the statue has been a popular spot for tourists since 2009, drawing visitors who come to take pictures with it.

Muhammadu Buhari became Nigeria’s leader by winning an election, not by force like he did last time. This election was one of the most competitive in the country’s history for five key reasons. First, it was the first time in Nigeria’s history that the opposition party beat the party in power through a fair vote. Buhari, who is 72 years old, won the presidency by getting about two million more votes than the current president, Goodluck Jonathan. This result matters because Nigeria is Africa’s largest country by population and economy, and it is one of the continent’s top oil producers. It also sends a lot of crude oil to the United States.

People around the world were celebrating as if Iran had just won the World Cup, but this event was even more important. Young Iranians celebrated in the streets by waving flags from their car sunroofs, playing loud music, and talking online using the hashtag #IranTalks. This excitement happened because Iran reached a major nuclear agreement with the United States and other countries. This deal is expected to end Iran’s isolation and remove strict economic sanctions that have hurt the country for years. Just before midnight on Thursday, Vali Asr street, a main road in Tehran, became like a street party. Drivers honked their horns, men danced in the traffic, and some people showed off U.S. dollar bills.

A federal court in Brooklyn has charged a fourth man, Dilkhayot Kasimov, with helping terrorists and with some of the men joining ISIS. He was added to a new legal document that also charges three men who were already arrested: Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, Akhror Saidakhmetov, and Abror Habibov. These three men are accused of supporting a foreign terrorist group and have said they are not guilty. It is not known if Kasimov has been caught yet.

The third "blood moon" in a series of four was the shortest eclipse, but it was still a nice sight for early morning viewers in North America. The moon moved completely into Earth’s shadow at 4:58 a.m. Pacific Time (7:58 a.m. Eastern Time) on Saturday. This started a total lunar eclipse that lasted nearly five minutes. NASA says this will be the shortest total eclipse of the century. Before, during, and after the eclipse, the moon turned a burnt-orange color. This color is why total eclipses are called "blood moons."

Istanbul, Turkey (CNN) – People in Turkey were scared and confused on Tuesday. “What is happening? Why can’t I use the subway?” asked an older woman wearing a white headscarf and holding shopping bags. She was standing outside a closed entrance to one of Istanbul’s busiest subway stations. She was just one of millions of people affected by the biggest power outage in Turkey in over ten years. For several hours on Tuesday, many cities across the country lost electricity. Millions of people were impacted, including passengers stuck on stopped trains and subways.

During Holy Week, we are reminded of what the Bible says about fair wages. Isaiah 58:6 describes the kind of fast God wants: breaking injustice, stopping workplace exploitation, freeing the oppressed, and canceling debts.

McDonald’s decision to raise wages for 90,000 employees is a big win for fast-food workers and their supporters. By standing together, these workers are making it harder for profitable companies like McDonald’s to pay such low wages that keep workers in poverty.

California is facing a severe drought, and Governor Jerry Brown has ordered mandatory water cuts for the first time. These rules apply to residents, businesses, and farms. The state requires cities and towns to reduce their water usage by 25% over the next nine months. This reduction equals about 1.5 million acre-feet of water, which is roughly 325,000 gallons per acre. Governor Brown stated that keeping lawns green with daily watering is no longer possible and belongs in the past.

People in the UK are running out of time to decide who to vote for, as voting stations are getting ready to open across the country. This election could change how the government works. The campaign was very short, especially compared to the United States, where candidates usually spend years preparing their messages. The result might give power to Ed Miliband’s Labour Party, replacing David Cameron’s Conservative government, or it could lead to difficult negotiations as leaders try to form partnerships with smaller parties. However, we won’t know the outcome until the polls close late Thursday evening, local time.

This is the time of year when Christians around the world—more than 2 billion people—think about the death and resurrection of Jesus. Because of the recent killing of Christian college students in Kenya and the ongoing danger to Christians in other countries, we are asking Christians this Holy Week to also remember those who have suffered. Many Christians, as well as other people, have been crucified, beheaded, stoned, enslaved, sexually abused, trafficked, harassed, bombed, or forced to leave their homes. These attacks happen simply because of their faith, which makes them targets for religious extremists.

The Washington Post released racist and offensive emails from three employees in Ferguson, Missouri, who have either quit or been fired. These messages were found during a U.S. Justice Department investigation into racial bias in the city’s police and courts. The emails contain offensive comments about President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, Muslims, and minorities. The Washington Post obtained the emails on Thursday through a public records request, and CNN reviewed them on Friday. The emails involve Police Captain Rick Henke and Sergeant [name cut off].

Two people, including a licensed greyhound trainer, were arrested in Australia after police found at least 55 dead dogs dumped in the bush in Queensland. According to reports from Australian media, the two suspects are a 71-year-old man and a 64-year-old woman from Bundaberg. The broadcaster ABC reported that both were charged with illegally possessing a firearm. The woman was also charged with obstructing police. Michael Beatty, who speaks for RSPCA Queensland, told ABC that the investigation is still ongoing. The animal rights group is helping Queensland police with their inquiry.

Two years ago, Mike Premeau and Kathy Danke started a small business called Memories Gourmet Pizza Co. in their town in Wisconsin. They were successful, getting their frozen pizzas—including breakfast and gluten-free varieties—into stores in Nichols, which is west of Green Bay. They also built up a group of loyal customers.

However, this week, their business was threatened because people confused them with Memories Pizza of Walkerton, Indiana. That other business made national news after its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding. As a result, angry people left comments on Memories Gourmet Pizza’s Facebook page and called their phone number to protest.

Archaeologists from the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna found the complete skeleton of a camel under a cellar in Tulln, Austria. The bones were discovered in 2006 and 2007 while workers were building a shopping center. At first, experts thought the skeleton belonged to a large horse or cow. However, Alfred Galik, an archaeozoologist, identified it as a camel by looking at its neck bones, lower jaw, and hand bones. This camel is believed to have been used by Ottoman soldiers who tried to capture Vienna in the 17th century.

Andrew Getty, 47, the grandson of J. Paul Getty, died on Tuesday afternoon at his home in Los Angeles. His parents, Ann and Gordon Getty, released a statement confirming the death and asking that the media and public respect the family’s privacy during this difficult time.

According to Ed Winter, assistant chief of the Los Angeles County coroner’s office, Getty’s death appears to have been caused by natural factors or an accident. Investigators found some medication at Getty’s home, but they do not know if he was taking it or what his medical history was.

We may never fully understand why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps on March 24, killing everyone on the plane. A recent report shows that he made the plane descend faster than it should have. This is a scary situation. As investigators look into what happened, we will find out more about how much Lubitz hid about his mental health and how much help he asked for. We need to ask how his depression affected his ability to fly. Should he have stopped working as a pilot? Should his doctors have warned others? His case highlights important questions about how people with mental illness are treated and the shame they often feel.

As his military career comes to an end, Britain’s Prince Harry is going to spend time in Australia. The 30-year-old prince arrives on Monday for a four-week visit with the Australian military. According to the Australian Defence Forces, he will work and live with Australian Army soldiers in several units in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth. A spokesman said that Harry has already spent time with Australian troops several times during his 10 years in the military.

According to the Florida Attorney General’s office, two current Florida prison guards and one former guard trainee have been charged with plotting to kill a former inmate who was about to be released. The men are Thomas Jordan Driver, 25; David Elliot Moran, 47; and Charles Thomas Newcomb, 42.

An FBI informant met them after going undercover in a group called the Traditional American Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, as reported by CNN affiliate WJXT. Court documents state that Driver told the informant he had fought with the inmate and that he and Moran wanted the inmate dead.

On Thursday in Lausanne, Switzerland, a group of world powers called the P5+1 finished a long and unpredictable series of talks with Iran. They reached a basic agreement on Iran’s nuclear program. However, it is not yet clear if this agreement will succeed. The two sides have until the end of June to work out the details and write the final plan. Even so, these talks were historic, especially because relations between the United States and Iran have been frozen for a long time. The negotiations were not glamorous. Instead, they showed what diplomacy can look like when it is both very good and very chaotic.

On Monday morning, an improvised bomb exploded near a United Nations vehicle in Garowe, a city in northeastern Somalia. The attack killed six people, including four aid workers from UNICEF, the international children’s agency. Somalia’s President called the bombing an attack on the country’s future. This event happened just one day after three African Union soldiers were killed in an ambush in Somalia’s Lower Shabelle region. The terrorist group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for Monday’s attack, which took place around 8 a.m. in Garowe, the administrative capital of the Puntland region.

Prince Harry arrived in Australia on Monday to spend four weeks working with the country’s military. Before starting his duties, the 30-year-old visited the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, the capital city. He paid his respects at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier.

A crowd gathered outside the memorial. Some people took photos of him, and one boy held up a sign that said, "Red Heads Rule!" to celebrate the prince's red hair.

According to the Australian Defence Forces, Harry will live and work with soldiers from the Australian Army in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth.

Australia, a key ally of the United States, has agreed to share some intelligence with Iran. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop described the deal as an "informal arrangement" focused on tracking Australians who travel to Iraq to fight for ISIS. However, one Australian lawmaker called the move "dancing with the devil." Over the weekend, Bishop became the first Australian government minister to visit Iran in 12 years, meeting with President Hassan Rouhani. The intelligence-sharing deal was announced in an interview released on Monday, which Bishop gave to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation while she was in Tehran.

Tests on the flight data recorder from Germanwings Flight 9525 show that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz intentionally made the plane go down faster, according to the French air accident investigation agency (BEA). The recorder, often called the "black box," was found on Thursday by recovery teams who had been searching the French Alps for days since the crash on March 24. The BEA said its team started looking at the data immediately.

A 110-day chase of a suspected illegal fishing boat ended in an unusual way when conservationists rescued the crew of the vessel they were pursuing. The environmental group Sea Shepherd had been following the ship, named the *Thunder*, since it was spotted in the Southern Ocean several months ago. The *Thunder* is wanted by Interpol for suspected fraud and fisheries crimes. The chase ended early Monday in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of West Africa, when the *Thunder* sent a distress call to the Sea Shepherd ship, the *Bob Barker*.

Most days, 16-year-old Jason Zobott goes to Huntley High School in suburban Chicago around 7:30 a.m., just like other high school students. However, what he does after that is unusual.

Jason is part of a blended learning program at his school. This program mixes online lessons with traditional classroom teaching. One-third of the school’s 2,700 students are in this program. By 2015, the school hopes to enroll most of its students in it.

Jason, who is a top-ranked junior, says the online work is easy to access. He balances a lot of schoolwork with many extracurricular activities. He says, “I can learn on my own.”

Days after a deadly Al-Shabaab attack in Garissa, Kenya, launched airstrikes against the terror group in Somalia. A military source confirmed the strikes but said they were not revenge for last week’s massacre at Garissa University College, which killed nearly 150 people. The source stated that these attacks are part of ongoing military operations that began in 2011, not a response to the recent tragedy. The source spoke to the media anonymously, which is standard practice for Kenyan military officials.

Pope Francis used his traditional speech after Easter Mass to remind the world that the Vatican is a country and that he acts as a moral leader. He spoke about the pain people are feeling in current wars and asked for all violence to stop. He specifically called for an end to the fighting in Iraq and Syria and for help to reach those who need it. He said, "May the international community not stand by before the immense humanitarian tragedy unfolding in these countries and the drama of the numerous refugees." This speech, known as "urbi et orbi" (which means "to the city of Rome and to the the world"), was delivered in Latin.

Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh, a 29-year-old U.S. citizen, did not enter a plea during his first court hearing on Thursday. He faces charges for allegedly helping terrorists. Al Farekh was sent from Pakistan to the United States. According to court documents, he is accused of planning to fight against U.S. forces overseas. CNN counterterrorism analyst Philip Mudd called the news something to celebrate.

Saudi state media reported on Thursday that a Saudi border guard was killed in a gunfight with militants in Yemen this week. This is the first known military death for Saudi Arabia since it started bombing rebels in its southern neighbor.

The fighting happened on Wednesday night in the Asir region of southwestern Saudi Arabia. Militants in the mountains on the Yemeni side shot at Saudi border troops, who then shot back. The guard, identified as Cpl. Salman Ali Yahya al-Maliki, was killed. Ten other people were injured, but their injuries were not life-threatening.

I was a little nervous when I went to the Al Marmoum camel race in Dubai. Because I am the only person from the Gulf countries on the CNN team, people expected me to know about camel racing, which is an old tradition in this area. Even though I tried to wear a kandora, which is traditional clothing in the United Arab Emirates, I still felt like an outsider because my way of thinking is modern. A friendly farm owner took us into the majlis, which is a place for meetings. The large room looked like a fancy theater. The camel owners sat on the floor and ate a’aish, a traditional Arabic dish made of fish and rice. Everyone was talking loudly and excitedly.

Havana, Cuba (CNN) – Charlie Hill sits in a dark bar on a bright, sunny day in Havana. He speaks with a rough voice and nods, showing he knows you have been looking for him. In fact, many people have been looking for Charlie Hill for a long time. For 43 years, Cuba has protected Hill from charges that he killed a police officer in New Mexico and hijacked an airplane to Havana. Now 65, Hill agreed to speak with CNN after we spent two years trying to contact him. He wants to talk about how he is now considering leaving his safe home in Cuba and returning to the United States.
